slides: Open the lecture by naming the chapter's unifying problem: surfaces are not only drawn, they are measured by invariants. The source span is short, so the deck should move quickly from classification to coloring. Emphasize that every later color count is ultimately constrained by Euler characteristic and orientability.

Use the route slide as a contract with the audience. The lecture will not attempt a full proof of every famous theorem; instead it makes the chapter's computational spine visible. Surfaces give the stage, regular maps provide incidence bookkeeping, and face-adjacency graphs translate geography into coloring.

For this slide, slow down on the two surface-building moves. A handle keeps a local frame coherent and lowers chi by two, while a cross-cap introduces one-sided behavior and lowers chi by one. The table is not a taxonomy for memorization; it is a compact calculator for later bounds.

Treat orientability as an experiment rather than a label. Ask students to imagine carrying a small arrow around a closed track. On the torus the arrow returns compatible with itself; on a Mobius-type strip it returns reversed. The artifact's dot products make that visual test numerically inspectable.

This is the algebraic heart of regular maps. Count face-edge, edge-vertex, and Euler incidences from the same cell decomposition, then solve for the common scale parameter. The torus exception is conceptually important because chi equals zero makes the counting equation lose a finite denominator.

The four-color problem enters through translation. A map on the sphere becomes a graph whose vertices are regions and whose edges mean shared boundary arcs. The tetrahedral example explains why four colors can be necessary, while the deck deliberately avoids pretending to reprove the modern theorem.

Present the six-color theorem as the elementary proof the chapter can own. Euler's formula forces a face with at most five neighbors on positive-characteristic surfaces. Remove that face, color the remaining map by induction, then return it with a color not used by its neighbors.

The Heawood expression looks mysterious until it is read as a tuned induction budget. The quadratic relation is chosen so the average-face inequality again produces a removable region with fewer forbidden colors than the budget. Point out the floor operation and the dependence on chi.

Complete graphs explain sharpness because every pair of regions is forced to touch. When K_n is realizable as a face-adjacency witness on a surface, n colors are not optional. The Klein bottle exception is worth naming because it prevents students from confusing a sufficient formula with universal sharpness.

Close by returning to the chapter's main method. Euler characteristic, orientability, incidence counts, and graph coloring are not separate topics; they are a pipeline from surface topology to map-coloring constraints. The useful habit is to ask which invariant is being spent at each step.
